name: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate

lead: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate (MAP) is a water-soluble vitamin C derivative used in serums and creams for a brighter, more even complexion and a fresher look. It is promoted as more stable than pure ascorbic acid.

It is described as a pro-drug: it is meant to convert to ascorbic acid after reaching the skin, where it acts as an antioxidant and reduces melanin. Lab work shows ascorbyl esters are more stable than the free acid in formulations, with skin penetration the main challenge. One small study reported improved skin hydration with a MAP product, and reviews note that clinical data on topical vitamin C are limited overall.

paras: It is used as a daily serum or cream, often in the morning under sunscreen, and is a common pick for people whose skin dislikes pure ascorbic acid. Brightening is typically judged over weeks of consistent use.
A cosmetic safety assessment covering MAP was published in 2005. It is sold without prescription; labels advise external use and avoiding the eyes.

chain: Converts to vitamin C in skin
angle.text: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate is a stable vitamin C pro-drug used in brightening serums for even tone and a fresher look. It converts to vitamin C in skin, giving antioxidant action and reduced melanin. It is common in products, with few direct human trials.

lead: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate (MAP) is a water-soluble derivative of vitamin C used as an ingredient in skincare products, where it is marketed as a more stable alternative to L-ascorbic acid. It is described in the literature as a pro-drug of vitamin C, meaning it is meant to be converted to ascorbic acid after reaching the skin. [1]

Laboratory work has found that ascorbic acid and its derivatives are more stable as ascorbyl esters than as the free acid in solution and in topical formulations. [2] A cosmetic ingredient safety review covering ascorbic acid and several of its salts and phosphate esters, including MAP, was published in the International Journal of Toxicology in 2005. [3]

Evidence for MAP specifically on appearance outcomes is limited. One small formulation study reported improved skin hydration with a MAP product, while a broader review of topical vitamin C notes that clinical studies of topical formulations are limited and that stability and penetration are the main challenges. [4][5]
infobox: Vitamin C derivative (phosphate ester, magnesium salt)
Cosmetic ingredient; reviewed in a cosmetic safety assessment [3]

paras: MAP appears in serums, creams and masks marketed for brightening, antioxidant protection and anti-aging. Reviews of topical vitamin C describe antioxidant, photoprotective, collagen-related and pigment-reducing effects for the vitamin as a class, though these reviews note that clinical data on formulated topical products are limited. [5]

L-ascorbic acid is unstable in solution, which motivated the development of derivatives. A 1997 analytical study found that ascorbyl palmitate and MAP were more stable than ascorbic acid in standard solutions and topical formulations. [2]

Percutaneous absorption research on pig skin examined ascorbic acid and its derivatives to define formulation features that deliver vitamin C into skin. [6] An in vitro study found that lasers and microdermabrasion increased skin permeation of vitamin C and also examined MAP delivery. [1] A 2019 study reported that hyaluronic acid microneedles were fabricated to enhance MAP delivery into skin. [7]

A Cosmetic Ingredient Review-style safety assessment of ascorbic acid, its calcium, magnesium and sodium salts, and magnesium and sodium ascorbyl phosphate, as used in cosmetics, was published in 2005. [3] Individual products carry their own label warnings, for example external use only and avoiding eye contact.

Published human data on MAP are sparse. A study comparing ascorbic acid, MAP and ascorbyl tetra-isopalmitate applied to forearm skin for four weeks in volunteers reported that all formulations increased stratum corneum hydration; only the ascorbic acid product changed transepidermal water loss, and the MAP product changed a skin elasticity ratio. The authors concluded MAP improved hydration while derivatives did not match ascorbic acid on water loss. In laboratory antioxidant tests in the same study, ascorbic acid was strongest in the water-based system. [4]
Registered clinical trials listing MAP are dental gel studies for periodontitis and peri-implantitis rather than cosmetic studies. [8][9]
